Hi Nick,

Thanks very much for your help on the first question.

Yes, I tried:

X [i, 1] <- x[i]
X [i, 2] <- x[i]

y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[i, 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])

and it worked perfectly. Thank you!

I tried the LW filter but still with no success (estimated parameters are wrong). The code I used for LW filter is shown below. I wonder why the LW filter is not working, now even with the correct model and nimble code.

I prefer the LW filter because it estimates the top-level parameters (usually not known for my applications) as well as the latent variable. Years ago, I implemented an EM algorithm for a state space model but it was really time-consuming due to analytical derivations (sometimes not working well). In this regard, nimble's PF's are intriguing.

Another thing I note is about the output of the LW filter. I only get a matrix of  # of particles times # of  params from mvEWSamples. For example,

LWFEWSamp <- as.matrix(cLWF$mvEWSamples)

#colnames (LWFEWSamp)

#[1] "d[1]"    "r11[1]"  "r12[1]"  "r22[1]"  "sigw[1]" "x[1]"

summ = apply (LWFEWSamp[5000:10000,], 2, mean)
> summ
       d[1]      r11[1]      r12[1]      r22[1] tau_sigw[1]        x[1]
 0.10635166  0.03532084  0.03577194  3.95894803  2.15448328  4.82565197

I expected the latent variable "x" itself would have (as an output of filtering) # of particles times # of t (in my case 136). But here I only get a single column variable for x (i.e., x[1]). In my non-PF code, I get x[1], x[2], ..., x[136], each with 50000 samples. Maybe I missed something here. If you could correct me on this, I would appreciate it.

Thank you again.

- Seongeun

> Hi Seongeun,
>
> Thanks a lot for posting your model and error!  I haven't yet tried the LW filter on your code, but for the second issue you posted, the following may help:
>
> In your model code,  you define:
>
> X [1] <- x[i]
> X [2] <- x[i]
>
> which then get used in the multivariate normal observation equation version of your model.  However, since BUGS (and thus NIMBLE's modeling language) is a declarative language, creating a single length 2 variable in your model (X) to contain all of the x[i] values from all time points will not work as expected.  That is, even though X[1] and X[2] are defined, and seemingly updated, within a for loop, their values will not necessarily be updated correctly as the MCMC algorithm runs.  To ensure that the correct values of x[i] are being passed in as the mean to the multivariate normal distribution, something like
>
> X [i, 1] <- x[i]
> X [i, 2] <- x[i]
>
> y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[i, 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])
>
> inside the for loop will work.  After this change, running your code again using NIMBLE's default MCMC gave posterior distributions for cR that seem to plausibly align with the MLE values you posted above.  Note that I used the following parameters to run the model:
>
> USE_PRECISION = TRUE
> USE_CHOL = FALSE
>
> Let me know if you try this and it does (or doesn't!) allow you include the off-diagonal covariance term successfully in your model.  I'll also try to investigate the LW filter and see if I can figure out what's happening there.
>
> Thanks!
>
> Nick

> >
> > Separately, I analytically derived the Kalman filter solution for this model (here I didn't include the drift term - seems to have minimal impact in this case - to make the math simpler), wrote its implementation in R and got a similar result to that of Shumway and Stoffer:

> > This suggests to me that Shumway & Stoffer's estimates are correct.

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to write a model that includes a multivariate normal part, with no correlations in SIGMA, but I keep running into a few problems. Code for a toy example is below.

1). Upon model building, I get an error message about the "leading minor of order 1 is not positive definite".
2). Also upon model building I get a message that the model is not fully initialized. I assume this is not a problem, since inits are supplied later, in the call to runMCMC.
3). Upon attempting to running the model (anyway), an output object is created, and the values seem reasonable.

I tried 2 different model statements that I understood to be equivalent, but maybe they are not:
Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cov=SIGMA[1:2,1:2])
Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cholesky=SIGMA[1:2,1:2],prec_param=0)

The first, but not the second statement produces the following error:
Error in chol.default(model$SIGMA[1:2, 1:2]) :
  the leading minor of order 1 is not positive definite

So my questions are:
1. Why does that error about the leading minor appear with the first, but not the second model statement, and why does it appear at all?
2. Am I correct in thinking that there is no need to worry about the initialization message, because inits are provided in the call to runMCMC?? Note that executing "model$initializeInfo()" produces slightly different results for the two model variants.
3. Is my prior specification for SIGMA valid? I wanted to specify a prior on sigma, then just fill in a matrix SIGMA for the MV normal.
4. If it is valid, do I still have to specify inits for SIGMA, or just for sig (used to populate SIGMA)?

Thanks,
Glenn

A toy example:
library(nimble)
library(mvtnorm)
# generate data
Y <- rmvnorm(25,c(300,350),sigma=matrix(c(9,0,0,9),2,2,byrow=TRUE))
# specify the model
nModel <- nimbleCode({
    for(j in 1:N){
        #Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cholesky=SIGMA[1:2,1:2],prec_param=0)
        Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cov=SIGMA[1:2,1:2])
    }
# priors and derivations
    sig ~ dgamma(3,1)
    for(i in 1:2){
        for(k in 1:2){
            SIGMA[i,k] <- equals(i,k)*sig*sig
        }
        mu[i] ~ dnorm(300,1/25)
    }
})
# monitors, constants, data, inits, and mcmc controls
parameters <- c("mu","sig")
nConsts <- list(N=25)
nInits <- function(){list(mu=rnorm(2,300,10),
               sig=rgamma(1,3,1),
               SIGMA=diag(rgamma(2,3,1)**2))}
nData <- list(Y=Y)
ni <- 300
nt <- 3
nb <- 100
nc <- 3
# compile and run the model
nim <- nimbleModel(code=nModel,name='nim',constants=nConsts,data=nData)
nimMCconf <- configureMCMC(nim,monitors=parameters,thin=nt)
nimMC <- buildMCMC(nimMCconf)
Cnim <- compileNimble(nim)
CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)
out <- runMCMC(CnimMC,niter=ni+nb,nburnin=nb,nchains=nc,inits=nInits)

Glenn, let me try to address your observations and questions briefly but accurately.

1). That is correct, you do.  That's because when you provide the "cov=SIGMA[,]" argument to dmnorm(), under the hood NIMBLE straight away re-parameterizes the dmnorm() distribution into another distribution called dmnorm_chol(), which is parameterized in terms of the mean (the same), and the cholesky factorization of the covariance matrix, that is, chol(SIGMA[,]).  When it does this, it tries to populate the value for this new parameter, let's call it chol_SIGMA[,].  It tries to populate that parameter value with chol(SIGMA[,]).  Since you don't provide an initial value for SIGMA, it's a 2x2 array of NA's.  So that chol() function produces that message: "leading minor of order 1 is not positive definite".

2). The message that the model is not fully initialized is ok.  That's because you don't provide initial values, as we've discussed.  It's up to you whether you want to provide them now, at the time of model building, or later, at the time of runMCMC().  It's not necessarily a bad idea to provide them at the time of model building, to make sure you haven't forgotten anything.  You can double-check this with a call to nim$calculate(), and make sure that returns a real number.  If so, then you know your model is good-to-go for the MCMC; while otherwise, you're relying / hoping that you remembered initial values for everything when you call runMCMC(), which might not be the case.

3). Yes, the model is still created, despite not being fully initialized.

Your questions:

1. Discussed above.  When you write the model the other way, supplying the chol and prec_param arguments, no reparameterizations or chol() calculations take place at the time of model building, hence no warning messages.

2. Yes, like I said, you can ignore the warning about model initialization, so long as you're very careful to provide proper initial values in the call to runMCMC().  I, personally, always prefer to fully initialize models at model-build-time, then move forward with confidence from there.  The reason you see different outputs from nim$initializeInfo() is that when you use the parameterization chol=SIGMA[,], since you (yourself) go directly to the (mean, chol, prec_param) parametization of dmnorm(), no reparameterization under-the-hoold is necessary, hence no "lifted" node (the one called "lifted_chol_oPSIGMA_oB1to2_comma_1to2_cB_cP") is ever created, and that's why it's absent from the information returned from nim$initializeInfo().

3. Yes, your prior specification for SIGMA is valid, although the initial values you provide for SIGMA (diag(rgamma(2,3,1)**2)) will be immediately over-written by the (model code) deterministic declaration of SIGMA:

for(k in 1:2){
            SIGMA[i,k] <- equals(i,k)*sig*sig
        }

Incidentally, this model declaration of SIGMA (inside the model code) can be simplified to read as:
SIGMA <- diag(rep(sig, 2))

4. Answered above.  The initial value for SIGMA is technically put into the model (for SIGMA) briefly, but it's over-written with the diagonal matrix diag(rep(sig, 2)) immediately as soon as one of many things happen (a model check, or nim$calculate() or beginning running the MCMC).

I think this addresses everything, probably in too much detail..  Let me know if anything is unclear.

Good luck!
Daniel

On Mon, Oct 1, 2018 at 3:28 PM Glenn Stauffer <gesta...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I am trying to write a model that includes a multivariate normal part, with no correlations in SIGMA, but I keep running into a few problems. Code for a toy example is below.
>
> 1). Upon model building, I get an error message about the "leading minor of order 1 is not positive definite".
> 2). Also upon model building I get a message that the model is not fully initialized. I assume this is not a problem, since inits are supplied later, in the call to runMCMC.
> 3). Upon attempting to running the model (anyway), an output object is created, and the values seem reasonable.
>
> I tried 2 different model statements that I understood to be equivalent, but maybe they are not:
> Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cov=SIGMA[1:2,1:2])
> Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cholesky=SIGMA[1:2,1:2],prec_param=0)
>
> The first, but not the second statement produces the following error:
> Error in chol.default(model$SIGMA[1:2, 1:2]) :
>   the leading minor of order 1 is not positive definite
>
> So my questions are:
> 1. Why does that error about the leading minor appear with the first, but not the second model statement, and why does it appear at all?
> 2. Am I correct in thinking that there is no need to worry about the initialization message, because inits are provided in the call to runMCMC?? Note that executing "model$initializeInfo()" produces slightly different results for the two model variants.
> 3. Is my prior specification for SIGMA valid? I wanted to specify a prior on sigma, then just fill in a matrix SIGMA for the MV normal.
> 4. If it is valid, do I still have to specify inits for SIGMA, or just for sig (used to populate SIGMA)?
>
> Thanks,
> Glenn
>
> A toy example:
> library(nimble)
> library(mvtnorm)
> # generate data
> Y <- rmvnorm(25,c(300,350),sigma=matrix(c(9,0,0,9),2,2,byrow=TRUE))
> # specify the model
> nModel <- nimbleCode({
>     for(j in 1:N){
>         #Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cholesky=SIGMA[1:2,1:2],prec_param=0)
>         Y[j,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:2],cov=SIGMA[1:2,1:2])
>     }
> # priors and derivations
>     sig ~ dgamma(3,1)
>     for(i in 1:2){
>         for(k in 1:2){
>             SIGMA[i,k] <- equals(i,k)*sig*sig
>         }
>         mu[i] ~ dnorm(300,1/25)
>     }
> })
> # monitors, constants, data, inits, and mcmc controls
> parameters <- c("mu","sig")
> nConsts <- list(N=25)
> nInits <- function(){list(mu=rnorm(2,300,10),
>                sig=rgamma(1,3,1),
>                SIGMA=diag(rgamma(2,3,1)**2))}
> nData <- list(Y=Y)
> ni <- 300
> nt <- 3
> nb <- 100
> nc <- 3
> # compile and run the model
> nim <- nimbleModel(code=nModel,name='nim',constants=nConsts,data=nData)
> nimMCconf <- configureMCMC(nim,monitors=parameters,thin=nt)
> nimMC <- buildMCMC(nimMCconf)
> Cnim <- compileNimble(nim)
> CnimMC <- compileNimble(nimMC,project=nim)
> out <- runMCMC(CnimMC,niter=ni+nb,nburnin=nb,nchains=nc,inits=nInits)
>

messages.body_plain:
Yes, yes, I was omitting the indexing for brevity.  Inside the model code, you'll always need full indexing (SIGMA[1:2,1:2]), *unless* you also supply the "dimensions" argument to the nimbleModel() function, in this case:

nim <- nimbleModel(..., dimensions = list(SIGMA = c(2,2))   )   ## indicate SIGMA is a 2x2 matrix

in which case you could just use SIGMA[,] inside your model code.

Also, I noticed the typo in my suggested simplification using diag(), it should rather use sig^2 to agree with your original code:

SIGMA[1:2,1:2] <- diag(rep(sig^2, 2))

Otherwise, I'm glad it all made sense!  And truly, the ability to supply inits to runMCMC() is truly the *secondary* place you might provide inits, mostly for the purpose of supplying *different* initial values when running multiple MCMC chains (e.g., runMCMC(..., nchains = 3))... that functionality was added long after the *primary* place you might supply model "inits", right when you build the model, in the function nimbleModel(code, constants, data, inits = list(...)).

Cheers!
Daniel

nim <- nimbleModel(..., dimensions = list(SIGMA = c(2,2))   )   ## indicate SIGMA is a 2x2 matrix

in which case you could just use SIGMA[,] inside your model code.

Also, I noticed the typo in my suggested simplification using diag(), it should rather use sig^2 to agree with your original code:

SIGMA[1:2,1:2] <- diag(rep(sig^2, 2))

Cheers!

Daniel

About the idea of writing x[i] and y[i] as the stochastic nodes, I think I follow what you are saying.  However I still think there might be a way to do it, either by how the distribution is written or how it is sampled.  In population dynamics state-space models, this makes a big difference.  Let me know if you want to follow up on this.

On to your question about the model declaration for Z[1]: The expression you gave seems to be a 1x2 matrix %*% a 2x2 matrix, which would give a 1x2 matrix, so I don't see how it could be a value for Z[1].  I may not be following what you said correctly.  I am looking at this in terms of code mechanics, not trying to follow your model's logic on this point.  Feel free to attach a reproducible example of this problem.  One issue that comes up in nimble is the need to match types in terms of scalar, 1D, 2D etc.  If you have a matrix expression to create a scalar, it will often actually return a 1x1 matrix or a length-1 vector, so you need to append [1, 1] or [1] to pick out the single element as a scalar, or other indices as needed.  E.g. "x[1:2] ~ (A[1:2, 1:2] %*% b[1:2])[1:2,].  The type behavior tries to mimic R, but R sometimes determines type at run-time, while allows it to make obvious conversions. Nimble must keep type static and determine it at compile-time.  Section 11.3 in the User Manual contains some detailed information on this kind of issue.  I'm not sure if this is part of what is tripping you up.  I'm just mentioning it because it is a source of confusion.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Perry,

I very much appreciate the assistance. I realize I left off part of sentence in my reply, apologies. What I meant to say is that when using step lengths and turning angles, I don't see an obvious way to not have the latent locations be a deterministic function of the step lengths and turning angles. But I'm sure there is a more efficient way to sample these latent quantities.

I'm certainly interested in learning how write efficient NIMBLE code. Our group (Quantitative Ecology Section of the USGS Western Fisheries Research Center) does a lot of work with JAGS, and I've taken on Stan, but this is my first foray into NIMBLE. I certainly appreciate the ability to implement other probability distributions, and the particle filter and sequential MC is what made me investigate it for this project, but clearly I have alot more learning to do before I attempt to use those samplers. I know the model I want to fit, but I clearly have a lot of questions in terms of implementation.

Your hint on running into a C-stack error, made me think about trying for a smaller version of the model. I was able to get a version of the model working on simulated data by reducing the number of observations. On my first run using this implementation of zero-inflation in step-lengths and turnings angles, I was not able to recover the simulated values. At first I thought that this could be due to inherent identifiability issues in resolving the process error and observation error. So I added in a third variable, "activity" which is assumed to be measured without error, but which is subject to hidden Markov dynamics. This comes directly from the applied problem I am trying to solve: we have a time series of GPS fixes taken every fifteen minutes on a forest carnivore. The GPS fixes are recorded with error, and about 25% of the time the GPS fixes fail altogether because the animal is in deep cover and the GPS is unable to see enough satellites to get a fix. However, for every attempt GPS fix we also have an "activity" measurement, which comes from an accelerometer on the GPS collar and which is a crude summary of how active the animal was in the interval between the current GPS fix and the previous one.

I was able to get the model including the activity part to run, but I ran into the same issue of not being able to recover the simulated values. However, if I leave out the state-space part of the model (i.e. no observation error) I am able to recover all of the hidden Markov model parameters (step length, turning angle, and transition matrix parameters). Similarly if I leave out the hidden Markov part of the model (i.e. behavioral states are known and treated as data) I am able to recover all of the state-space mode parameters (step length, turning angle, and observation error parameters). Crucially, if I leave out the zero-inflation but otherwise attempt to fit the combined hidden Markov state-space model, I am able to recover the parameters. In this case, the animal switches between a "reduced" movement state (short step lengths, diffuse turning angle) and an "active" movement state (long step lengths, more concentrated turning angles). I actually have this equivalent model working in Stan. My inability to figure out how to implement a version of the model in Stan where one of the movement states is a resting state with step lengths exactly equal to zero is what motivated me to take a look at NIMBLE. But it seems it's a tricky problem here as well.

My code in exploring NIMBLE for tackling this problem is attached. Part 5 is the example which does not work, all other parts are toy models in which I'm able to recover the parameters. If you have any advice on 1) (most crucially) allowing for a stationary resting state, meaning step-lengths of zero under this parameterization, 2) improving the sampling to avoid crashing or simply having the model fail to run, it would be very much appreciated. I'll continue to noodle around otherwise.

Regarding, my previous question about matrix multiplication in NIMBLE: I'm attempting to fit the initial distribution of the latent state in the hidden Markov model (z[1]) as a categorical variable where the probability of each category is given by the stationary distribution of the Markov process <https://brilliant.org/wiki/stationary-distributions/>. This is not critical, but it saves me having to estimate a single redundant parameter and helps me understand the quirks of NIMBLE. In my simulated example, I have the transition matrix:

  alpha[1, 1] <- remain[1] #probability of remaining in state 1, simulated as 0.95
  alpha[1, 2] <- 1 - remain[1] #probability of switching to state 2 if in state 1, = 0.05
  alpha[2, 1] <- 1 - remain[2] #probability of switching to state 1 if in state 2, = 0.1
  alpha[2, 2] <- remain[2] #probability of remaining in state 2, = 0.9

With those values, the stationary distribution is a [0.666, 0.333]. Meaning that two-thirds of the time we expect the animal to be in state 1. Because we don't know what state the animal is in prior to the first observation, it makes sense to parameterize the first state according to the stationary distribution. Currently, I'm simply allowing NIMBLE to estimate another parameter for the initial state:

  lambda[1] ~ dunif(0,1)

  lambda[2] <- 1 - lambda[1]

  z[1] ~ dcat(lambda[1:2]) ## assign behavioral mode for first obs

But I know that lamba should really be a function of alpha, hence the matrix math to get there. I was finally able to get a crude calculation to run that looks like this:
  invertible_alpha_trans[1, 1] <- 1 - alpha[1, 1] + 1
  invertible_alpha_trans[1, 2] <- 0 - alpha[1, 2] + 1
  invertible_alpha_trans[2, 1] <- 0 - alpha[2, 1] + 1
  invertible_alpha_trans[2, 2] <- 1 - alpha[2, 2] + 1

  inverse_alpha_tran[1:2, 1:2] <- inverse(invertible_alpha_trans[1:2, 1:2])[1:2, 1:2]

  lambda[1] <- inverse_alpha_tran[1, 1] - inverse_alpha_tran[1, 2]
  lambda[2] <- inverse_alpha_tran[2, 1] - inverse_alpha_tran[2, 2]

Aside from being ugly, when I attempt to fit that, the transition parameters appear to stay stuck at their initial values. This is small potatoes in terms of what I want to accomplish, but it strikes me as curious.

Side note: I ran into an error implementing this variable as a beta distribution which appears to be a bug. This works:
  for (t in 1:(N - 1))
    activity[t]   ~ dbeta(a[z[t]], b[z[t]])

but this causes an error, even though it should be equivalent:
  activity[1]   ~ dbeta(a[z[1]], b[z[1]])
  for (t in 1:(N - 2))
    activity[t + 1]   ~ dbeta(a[z[t + 1]], b[z[t + 1]])

Oddly, NIMBLE has no problem with this:

  steps[1]   ~ dgamma(shape[z[1]], rate[z[1]])

  for (t in 1:(N - 2))
    steps[i + 1]      ~ dgamma(shape[z[i + 1]], rate[z[i + 1]])

Thanks for reposting this on the users list.

This issue can be easily addressed, with a different workflow using NIMBLE's MCMC engine.

In short, every time you call the nimbleMCMC() function, it:
- Creates a new MCMC algorithm for your model
- Compiles that new MCMC algorithm, and links the newly-created DLL into R
- Executes this compiled MCMC algorithm, and gives you the results

As it goes, R has a maximum of (I believe) 100 linked DLLs in any given R session.  If you try to link in more than that, you get the error message you're seeing ("Error: Maximum DLLs reached").  So, we need to avoid compiling a new MCMC algorithm each time.  That's easy to avoid in NIMBLE, even with changing the model data, as you're doing.

Let me just provide an example of how to do this, on a simple model.

Note, importantly, the new workflow will be:

- create a single model object
- Create a single MCMC algorithm for your model
- Compile both the model and MCMC (only once!)
- Create a function that sets the data and initial values (covariate values) into the *compiled* model object, then
- Uses runMCMC to execute the *compiled* MCMC algorithm, and
- Returns the results

This simple example should quickly generalize to your model, but let me know if anything is unclear.

Cheers,

Daniel
NIMBLE Development Team

library(nimble)

code <- nimbleCode({
    a ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    y ~ dnorm(a, sd = sigma)
})

nReps <- 10

## separately generate response *data*,
## and *inits* for covariates, etc
data.gen <- function() {
    y <- rnorm(1)
    sigma <- runif(1)
    list(data = list(y=y),
         inits = list(sigma = sigma))
}

simu.data <- as.list(rep(NA, nReps))
for(i in 1:nReps) {
    simu.data[[i]] <- data.gen()
}

## supply data here, so that 'y' is specified as data,
## and no MCMC sampler is placed on y.
## we'll change the value of the data later, inside the loop
constants <- list()
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, constants, data = simu.data[[1]]$data)

conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, enableWAIC = TRUE)
conf$printSamplers()
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
Cmcmc <- compileNimble(Rmcmc, project = Rmodel)

    data.new <http://data.new> <- dat$data
    inits.new <http://inits.new> <- dat$inits
    Cmodel$setData(data.new <http://data.new>)
    Cmodel$setInits(inits.new <http://inits.new>)
    mcmc.out <- runMCMC(Cmcmc, nchains = 1, nburnin = 1000, niter = 10000,
                        summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE)
    list(mcmc.out$summary, mcmc.out$WAIC)
}

Thanks for that, Daniel.  Basically, if all you need to do is change values in a model, there is no reason to rebuild and recompile everything.

I'll add that another option for changing the data values is simply to change them using list-like access.

e.g. instead of
Cmodel$setData(data.new <http://data.new>)
you can have as much control as you want doing
Cmodel$y <- data.new <http://data.new>$y

This has the advantage that it is also the right way to change values of explanatory variables, whereas "setData" should really only be used for response variables.  In an uncompiled model, setData tells the model what variables should be flagged as data, in addition to assigning their actual values.

Finally, there is a way to clear DLLs from your session, but it remains a hidden feature for now.  It is:
nimble:::clearCompiled(Cmodel)

where the argument can be any object associated with a DLL, and then *all* compiled object associated with that DLL will be cleared.  nimbleMCMC does not call this, so you would have to use it in a workflow where you are calling compileNimble yourself. It is slightly dangerous because there could be conceivable ways to crash your system if you clear a DLL and then use an interface object that expects the DLL to be loaded, but we've *tried* to do it cleanly.  nimbleMCMC is just a simple wrapper for building, compiling and running an MCMC.  As soon as you step outside of vanilla uses, you'll generally need to do this handful of steps yourself to gain more control.

-Perry

Dear All,

In my earlier post ("Help for state space modeling using NIMBLE particle filter"), I shared my experiment for a state space model with two observations for each time step and got very helpful comments (Thank you!).

Now, I am trying to use the model to a data with missing values in observations (the same code is used, so I don't post here again).

Using data with NAs, I realize that when I used the observation (i.e., y) of size N x 2 with a covariance matrix (i.e., R) of 2 x 2 with correlation, the parameters for R are not sampled correctly. Without the correlation, as expected, the diagonal term of R was correctly sampled.

The R matrix was simply defined as:

R [1,1] <- pow (r11,2) # r11 & r22 are sd.

R [2,2] <- pow (r22,2)

R [1,2] <- rho*r11*r22

R [2,1] <- R [1,2]

rho ~ dunif (-1,1)

To figure this out, I filled the NA values with the means of the series (i.e.,  mean of y [,1] and mean of y[,2]), which is a simple method of imputation for missing data. Then I found that all the parameters were correctly estimated including the correlation parameters. From this, I conclude that the correlation parameters are affected by the missing data although NIMBLE seems to treat the missing observations well.

So, I added the following (in R script) to the "constants" to indicate whether each time step includes NA values or not:

is_Yfull = !is.na <http://is.na> (y)

is_Yfull = is_Yfull[,1]&is_Yfull[,2] # TRUE or FALSE

constants <- list(

    t = nrow (y), is_Yfull=is_Yfull

)

Now, in NIMBLE, I used it as follows:

for (i in 2:t) {

    ...

   yf <- is_Yfull[i]

   if (yf) {

       # if both y[i,1] and y[i,2] have non-NA values

       y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[i, 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])

   } else {

        # due to missing values in y, consider the on-diagonal only.

y [i,1] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[1,1]))

y [i,2] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[2,2]))

   }

   ...

}

Some of you may find the problem with my code immediately, but the error message I get is:

defining model...

Error in eval(code[[2]], constantsEnv) : object 'yf' not found

I wonder if there is a correct way to treat the missing observations, in particular to estimate the correlation parameters of R. I would appreciate it if you could offer any thoughts or comments.

Thank you very much.

- Seongeun

Right now I'm just responding on the mechanics of the last part of your message.  Looking at what should be happening regarding missing data is another issue.

You can't use an if-then like that in model code.  You can use an if-then if the condition can be evaluated *once* when the model is created and any variables in the condition are R variables.  You can't have model variables in the if statement.  The reason is that nimble creates a static graphical model.

There are a couple of ways to get the behavior you want.  One is to write a custom distribution, but that probably isn't necessary here.  Another is to use something like

for(i in 1:N_full) {
   y[ full_indices[i], 1:2] ~ ...
}

for(i in 1:N_not_full) {
  y[ not_full_indices[i], 1] ~ ...

Hi Seongeun,

Just a note to mention that you should in NIMBLE be able to use
y[ not_full_indices[i], 1:2 ] ~ dmnorm(X[not_full_indices[i], 1:2],

cov = R[1:2,1:2])

and NIMBLE would sample those y's from their predictive bivariate
normal distributions, if both elements of the two-element vector are
NA.
I don't know if that's what you want, but the MCMC should be valid. If
you think it is not, please provide us with a reproducible example.

We don't have a way, however, to handle a multivariate node that has
some NAs and some non-NAs, because NIMBLE can't sample
from the conditional of multivariate distribution for a subset of the elements.

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Neal,

First a note that the code you sent me off-list is slightly different than the code in the post. I'm attaching the code you sent here for the record.

1) As far as missing values, if you have a vector of data and include NA values in the vector, NIMBLE should treat the NAs as missing values. But I don't see any missing data in your dataset, so I'm not sure what you are referring to. Please see Section 6.1.1.3 of the manual.

2) There are some typos in your code (some of them only in the attached version):
a) simga2 -> sigma2
b) use of w vs W
c) This for loop:

for (j in i:K)

should loop over 1 to K not i to K.

3) As far as the problem with compilation,

a) You need diag(M), not diag(1, M). Our use of diag() is more restricted than R's. Please see Table 11.1 in the manual for what is allowed by NIMBLE.

b) This line won't work because you don't want vectorized multiplication.
mu[i,j]<-X[i,1:p]*beta[1:p,j]
Instead you can do:
mu[i,j] <- inprod(X[i,1:p], beta[1:p,j])

c)  In your old code, note that

X[i,1:p]%*%beta[1:p,j]

produces a matrix because %*% always produces a matrix in NIMBLE model or nimbleFunction code. In this case that is a 1x1 matrix, so you would need the following so that everything is treated as a scalar:
alpha[i,j] <-exp((X[i,1:p]%*%beta[1:p,j])[1,1]+W[i,j])

In general, if you get a compilation error, do use the flag "showCompilerOutput = TRUE". While it is often a bit hard to understand exactly it often indicates what  variable or line of code is causing the problem.

4) With the above changes, the MCMC runs but it quickly encounters numerical issues. Note that the values in your X matrix can be very large -- when you take such large values, multiply by beta and exponentiate, you get numerical overflow and the MCMC will fail. You should scale the X values to be smaller magnitude (e.g., by standardizing by the column means and standard deviations).

5) While your CAR specification should work, note the following:

a) It would be more efficient to represent the precision matrix of the dmnorm and not use the inverse() call. That would avoid having to invert the matrix every time rho or sigma values change.

b) More generally instead of  writing up the CAR "manually" as you do:
   w[1:M,i]~dmnorm(mean=mean_w[1:M],cov=cov_w[i,1:M,1:M])

   cov_w[i,1:M,1:M]<-sigma2[i]*inverse(diag(1,M)-rho[i]*adj[1:M,1:M])

you might use our dcar_proper distribution. Please see the chapter in the manual on spatial models.

-chris
